This makes the DNA more accessible. By adding the methyl group, the binding strength between the histones and DNA decreases, hence making it easier to transcribe genes. HDACs on the other hand, removes the acetyl group from the lysine residue, which causes the DNA to be more tightly bound with the histones. This makes the DNA harder to transcribe genes.   ### Histone Phosphorylation Histone phosphorylation occurs when kinases phosphorylate serine or threonine residues on the tails of the histones. When this happens, it makes the DNA less accessible as it loosens the histones' grip on the DNA. This makes it harder to transcribe genes.   ### Chromatin Remodeling Enzymes These enzymes break the hydrogen bonds between nucleotides in DNA. They also cleave crosslinks between bases and unwinds DNA. This allows the DNA to be more accessible, therefore making it easier to transcribe genes. Sources: Lecture

Promoters are cis-acting elements that recruit factors and enhancers are cis-acting elements that recruit RNA polymerase 2. Both are involved in gene expression but they have different roles. In eukaryotes, many genes are transcribed together in a process called polycistronic mRNA synthesis. This allows cells to make proteins that share similar functions at the same time. The enhancer element tells the cell where to start making the protein and which part needs to be made first. It also tells it how long it should take before stopping production of this particular protein. Promoter elements tell the cell when it needs to stop producing certain proteins. They also tell the cell what type of protein needs to be produced next. There are two types of promoter elements - strong and weak ones. Strong promoters are responsible for initiating transcription while weak ones just help with regulation. Weak promoters may not always work properly because some genes require specialized machinery to produce their products efficiently. However, strong promoters usually do work well since they are designed specifically for these purposes. Enhancers play a role in gene expression by helping to ensure that all parts of the gene are expressed equally. This means that if one section of the gene is deleted or mutated, other sections will still function normally. Enhancers also help maintain the integrity of chromosomal structure during replication. Chromosomal regions containing multiple copies of the same gene tend to break apart easily due to errors caused by damage to either strand of DNA. By providing additional support for these fragile areas, enhancers prevent them from becoming too fragmented. Finally, enhancers serve as landmarks for transcription factors (TFs) looking for specific sites along the length of the gene. TFs recognize specific patterns within the sequence of nucleotides forming each individual base pair. Once bound to these patterns, TFs activate nearby genes by stimulating the activity of nearby promoters. Promoters control whether or not a gene is turned on and off depending on environmental conditions. For example, when there is lots of food around, genes associated with digestion become active. On the other hand, when there isn't enough food available, genes related to starvation become dominant. Once the two strands have been copied, DNA proofreading enzymes recognise the mismatch between the thymine and uracil bases. Therefore, they remove the entire section of the newly synthesised strand containing the mismatched base pairs, resulting in a frame shift mutation. These are called spontaneous deamination errors. They are considered spontaneous because they occur without any external stimuli and they are caused by the intrinsic properties of the nucleobases. It is thought that the rate of spontaneous deamination errors varies from one organism to another due to differences in their metabolic activity and therefore amount of free radicals present. Spontaneous deamination errors are a major cause of cancer. This is because the mutations created allow tumour-suppressor genes to be turned off, allowing cells to divide uncontrollably. The function of the poly(A) tail is to protect the mRNA from exonuclease digestion, which would degrade it in the cytoplasm. Also, the poly(A) tail aids translation by binding to proteins that help recruit ribosomes to the mRNA. However, not all mRNAs have poly(A) tails; some mRNAs lack this tail (e.g. rRNA).
